Introduction


Over the past decade, the role of AI in scientific discovery has changed significantly. Early successes in AI for science came largely from specialized models that served as predictors or optimizers for well-defined scientific objects, such as protein structures, quantum wavefunctions, or molecular potentials [65, 21, 107, 151, 169]. More recently, language models have been treated as researchers, generating candidate solutions, writing and revising the programs that implement them, and carrying a line of inquiry across many steps in response to evaluator feedback [17, 48, 85, 100]. For instance, recent systems build the loop around evolutionary search procedures, as exemplified by AlphaEvolve and related approaches [100, 114, 6, 73], or around tree search [9], while other works adapt the model through test-time reinforcement learning on a single problem [155, 165]. Despite differences in domains, models, and search heuristics, these systems share a common building block: the propose-evaluate-refine discovery loop that drives new discovery results [114, 43, 123, 165].


Figure 1: Overview of SimpleTES.

(b) We explore applications spanning 28 open-ended discovery tasks across

(c) Representative state-of-the-art discoveries across these

(d) Trajectory-level post-training fine-tunes the generator on its own high-performing trajectories, crediting each attempt by the trajectory’s final outcome rather than its immediate score. It improves trajectory scores on both training and held-out tasks and establishes a new state of the art of 1.1448871.144887 on the held-out Sum–Difference Problem.


More broadly, the human research community advances science collectively by scaling this loop in a complex, decentralized manner: researchers around the world pursue candidate solutions in parallel, driven by different inspirations, test them against the current baselines, and use the resulting feedback to shape the next attempts [74].
With LLMs taking the role of individual researchers in the loop, the entire scaling can be designed completely differently: an organized, structured way to drive scientific breakthroughs more efficiently and effectively.
We name this new scaling dimension evaluation-driven scaling, because it is primarily driven by evaluation signals from empirical measurements, simulations, formal checks, or performance profiles, which later on become inspirations of next proposals.
Different from standard model scaling that scales up parameters and training data [67, 56], or classical test-time scaling that scales through longer reasoning traces or additional agent turns [129, 158, 96, 174, 83, 69],
evaluation-driven scaling targets challenging, open-ended problems that fundamentally require explorations, and a larger number of loops does not automatically imply better results.
While showing promise in making discoveries, existing systems leave unexamined how the loop itself should be organized in a structured way. This leads to a central question:
How can AI-driven discovery loops be scaled in a structured way to accelerate scientific breakthroughs?


This paper introduces SimpleTES (Simple Test-time Evaluation-driven Scaling), a framework for scaling AI-driven discovery by structuring how evaluator queries are allocated and how evaluated histories are grown, filtered, and reused. The central challenge is to determine how early attempts and their evaluation signals should guide later proposals, and which search structures allow progress to compound on open-ended problems. SimpleTES draws on structural features of scientific communities: locally, individual researchers test a few variants and carry forward the best; over time, researchers selectively learn from prior results based on relevance, performance, and reputation; collectively, researchers build on one another’s ideas to refine and propose new solutions; and in parallel, multiple lines of inquiry develop and compete. SimpleTES operationalizes these features through a compact and structured design tuple (C,L,K,Φ)(C,L,K,\Phi). Global width CC maintains independent trajectories, refinement depth LL lets feedback accumulate within each trajectory, local sample size KK filters candidate variants before they shape future refinement, and the proposal constructor Φ\Phi selects and compresses useful prior solutions, failures, and feedback into the next prompt. This reframes discovery-loop scaling as a problem of managing evaluated histories, so that additional evaluations compound into stronger trajectories rather than merely producing more attempts.
The key distinction between SimpleTES and existing AI discovery systems such as AlphaEvolve lies in the focus. Existing systems typically seek to maximize discovery performance through customized agentic search procedures. SimpleTES instead asks how the discovery loop itself should be organized and scaled. By isolating this structure, SimpleTES becomes a simple, structured, and highly parallelizable system that scales efficiently to tens of thousands of evaluator queries, yielding better results using smaller open-source models compared to prior systems that used larger proprietary LLMs.
A comprehensive comparison can be found in Supplementary B.1.


We apply SimpleTES on 28 open-ended problems across diverse scientific domains, spanning quantum circuit compilations, astrodynamics trajectory designs, GPU kernel implementation, LLM scaling law designs, biological and time-series algorithms optimization, and mathematical constructions.
On all problems, SimpleTES discovers the state-of-the-art solutions using a single open-source GPT-OSS model, surpasses both human experts and other AI discovery systems that use an order of magnitude larger proprietary models.
To illustrate, SimpleTES improves the best-known bound for the Erdős minimum-overlap problem, open in extremal combinatorics since 1955, ahead of every prior human and machine record [100]. It discovers quantum compilation policies that reduce expensive qubit-swap gates by over 20% relative to the widely used LightSABRE baseline [176]. It improves the fuel efficiency of Solar System exploration mission trajectories, reducing propulsive costs by up to 23% relative to references constructed from historical encounter sequences under the same orbital-dynamics evaluator [148, 121]. It implements the fastest TriMul kernel, the triangle multiplicative update central to AlphaFold3 [66, 1], and a lasso path solver 2.17×2.17\times faster than the widely used glmnet [39]. In neuroscience, it also discovers a state-of-the-art whole-brain neural-activity predictor, reducing error by 8.5%8.5\% on the long-horizon time-series forecasting task in ZAPBench [88] relative to the proprietary-model-driven algorithm discovery result [9]. More than any single record, what matters is that one unchanged procedure produces all of them, from abstract mathematical constructions to executable scientific programs, showing that SimpleTES can serve as a general mechanism for discovery.


The above results come from the fixed, off-the-shelf GPT-OSS model, which is not specifically optimized for the long-horizon discovery that SimpleTES performs: standard post-training tends to reward outputs that score well immediately, whereas discovery often turns on unconventional attempts that score poorly on their own yet lead to much stronger solutions. This raises a natural question: how can the LLM itself be deliberately trained for long-horizon discovery? We address this by post-training the model on its own successful trajectories, crediting each attempt by the final outcome of its trajectory rather than its immediate score. The improved model then drives the same search, now less myopic and more willing to build on early failures in pursuit of a stronger eventual solution. We study training primarily in mathematics, across a range of related open-ended problems. Post-training improves the entire outcome distribution, raising both the average score across independent trajectories and the best score on problems where the off-the-shelf GPT-OSS model scores poorly, and it transfers to held-out mathematical problems. These results suggest the trained model learns to search for strong eventual solutions rather than optimizing for immediate scores.


In summary, SimpleTES takes the scaling of the loop as its object of study, and asks how a fixed budget of evaluator queries should be structured. By formalizing this structured scaling with the design tuple (C,L,K,Φ)(C,L,K,\Phi), SimpleTES shows superior performance using the open-source model, surpassing existing systems that uses larger proprietary models.
SimpleTES uses a single configuration to handle all five domains and discover 28 SOTA results, with only the evaluator changing between problems.
A summary of SimpleTES result with the open-sourced model can be found in Table˜1.

Overview of SimpleTES 


SimpleTES is a test-time framework for scientific discovery on problems that have a verifiable evaluation protocol, which we call an evaluator. An evaluator is the system’s interface to the scientific objective: given a candidate solution, it returns a numerical score together with auxiliary feedback such as verifier messages, error traces, or runtime statistics. Depending on the task, it may compute the objective exactly (an exact verifier), estimate it empirically (a measurement), or approximate it (a heuristic proxy). The objective is to find the highest-scoring candidate under the evaluator.


Formally, a problem is specified by an instruction x0x_{0}, and the goal is a solution yy that maximizes the score rr output by an evaluator VV. To search for such a solution, an LLM GG plays the role of a researcher, drawing candidates y∼G​(x)y\sim G(x) from a proposal xx built from the instruction x0x_{0} together with the accumulated history of previously evaluated solutions, their scores, and the evaluator’s feedback. SimpleTES runs this as a propose–evaluate–refine loop: GG proposes a candidate, VV evaluates it, and its score and feedback are folded into the history that shapes the next proposal.


SimpleTES organizes this loop through a compact design tuple




(C,L,K,Φ),\displaystyle(C,L,K,\Phi),

(1)


where CC is the number of parallel trajectories, LL the number of refinement steps per trajectory, KK the number of candidates drawn per step, and Φ\Phi the proposal constructor that assembles each new proposal from a trajectory’s history. SimpleTES launches CC independent trajectories and advances each for LL refinement steps. At each step, Φ\Phi builds a proposal xx from the history so far, GG draws KK candidate solutions from xx, VV scores them, and the highest-scoring one is appended to the trajectory. Once every trajectory has completed, SimpleTES returns the best solution across all of them, having spent N=C×L×KN=C\times L\times K evaluator queries.


This decomposition is what gives SimpleTES its structure: each of the three dimensions targets a distinct, independent way an undirected search fails, so together they form a small and non-redundant set of controls on the search, which we analyse and ablate in the Methods. Refinement depth LL lets feedback accumulate, so later attempts build on earlier ones, but a single deep trajectory is not enough, since once early attempts bias the search toward a narrow direction, further refinement tends to reinforce that basin rather than escape it. Global width CC counters this by running independent trajectories in parallel, so competing directions mature without influencing one another early on. Local sample size KK addresses noise in the LLM’s output: drawing several candidates at each step and committing only the highest-scoring one keeps a weak or non-executable candidate from corrupting every later refinement built on it. Because the three act on different failure modes, they can be adjusted independently, and the budget NN has a clear meaning as the way that scaling is allocated.


In practice, the allocation of the evaluator-query budget across CC, LL, and KK depends on the task. Problems whose progress depends on discovering qualitatively different approaches, such as mathematical construction problems, benefit from larger CC, whereas problems dominated by incremental engineering refinement, such as GPU kernel optimization, benefit from larger LL. The local sample size KK should remain moderate: increasing it makes each committed step more reliable, but leaves fewer refinement steps under the same budget. Unless otherwise stated, we use C=32C=32, L=100L=100, and K=16K=16 as a default configuration.


While CC, LL, and KK govern how evaluated histories grow, the proposal constructor Φ\Phi governs which parts of that history are reused, since a trajectory’s history soon becomes too long and noisy to feed back in full. Because each proposal can build on several prior attempts rather than only the last, the history forms a directed graph rather than a chain. Φ\Phi selects which attempts to reuse through a graph-based variant of the PUCT rule [115, 127, 126], favoring attempts that scored well or led to strong later attempts, while still giving promising but rarely used ones a chance to be revisited. It also folds in a running summary of recurring failures, such as compilation errors, verifier failures, or timeouts, to steer GG away from unproductive directions.
In Methods, a Pólya-urn analysis together with ablations on CC, LL, and KK shows why these dimensions form a compact design space for scaling the loop, and Φ\Phi’s construction and selection strategy are specified and ablated in full. We next turn to the discoveries SimpleTES makes across scientific domains, and then to how a language model can be trained for SimpleTES-based discovery.

SimpleTES improves optimizers for fuel-efficient deep-space trajectories



Figure 3: Fuel-efficient deep-space mission design with evolved optimizers. (a) Task abstraction and prospective Jupiter-window example.
SimpleTES searches over encounter sequences, maneuver placement, and continuous trajectory variables such as event times.
Gravity assists reshape the heliocentric trajectory without propellant expenditure, whereas DSMs add fuel cost.
In the 2028–2030 launch window, SimpleTES identifies an evaluator-feasible trajectory that reaches Jupiter in 2035 with no intermediate DSMs.
(b) Historical mission-window comparisons.
References are constructed from the corresponding historical encounter sequences and evaluated under the same simplified patched-conic model, constraints, and cost definition as SimpleTES, rather than using flown mission Δ​v\Delta v budgets.
The evolved optimizers find lower same-evaluator propulsive cost in all five windows.
(c) Sources of improvement across the five historical benchmarks.
Timelines compare the encounter sequences and event times of each reference and best evolved trajectory; triangles mark DSMs of at least 10​m​s−110\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.
For Galileo and Rosetta, the gains come from sequence optimization with continuous-variable optimization; The improvement of Mariner 10, Voyager 2, and Cassini is from continuous-variable optimization within independently recovered reference sequences.


Deep-space missions often reach distant targets by using planets as moving gravitational waypoints rather than flying directly.
A gravity assist (GA) uses a planetary flyby to reshape the spacecraft’s heliocentric path with little propellant, whereas a deep-space maneuver (DSM) uses an engine burn to adjust the path [98].
Designing such missions is difficult because route choices and timing choices are tightly coupled: the optimizer must choose which bodies to encounter, which transfer branches to use, and where maneuvers may be inserted, while also setting launch and encounter epochs and maneuver variables [148, 121].
We formulate this as an evaluation-driven discovery task in which each candidate produced by SimpleTES is an executable mission-design program. Given mission windows, a target body, allowed flyby bodies, and endpoint conditions, the program proposes complete multi-gravity-assist trajectories (Figure˜3a); an independent patched-conic evaluator reconstructs the trajectory from ephemerides [38], transfer arcs [62], flybys [95], DSMs, and endpoint costs, rejects constraint violations, and scores feasible designs by verified propulsive cost.


We benchmark SimpleTES on five historical mission-window benchmarks and a prospective Jupiter exploration window.
For the historical benchmarks, the comparison is not to flown mission Δ​v\Delta v budgets, which incorporate operational choices, navigation margins, and mission-specific high-fidelity modeling.
Instead, each reference trajectory is constructed from the historical encounter sequence and nominal timing, then evaluated under the same orbital-dynamics model, feasibility constraints, and cost definition used to score SimpleTES.
Across the historical mission windows, the best verified trajectories found by the discovered optimizers reduce propulsive cost in every case, by 2.1–23.1% relative to these same-evaluator references (Figure˜3b). In the prospective 2028–2030 Jupiter exploration window, where no encounter sequence is prescribed, the discovered optimizer synthesizes an evaluator-feasible no-DSM Earth–Venus–Earth–Earth–Jupiter trajectory reaching Jupiter in 2035 (Figure˜3a).


Inspection of the evolved optimizers shows that the gains arise from reusable policies for coupled discrete–continuous mission design.
The clearest sequence-level changes occur for Galileo and Rosetta (Figure˜3c): the Galileo optimizer finds Earth–Venus–Venus–Venus–Earth–Jupiter rather than the reference Earth–Venus–Earth–Earth–Jupiter sequence, while the Rosetta optimizer finds Earth–Earth–Earth–67P rather than Earth–Earth–Mars–Earth–Earth–67P.
For Mariner 10, Voyager 2, and Cassini, the programs independently recover the reference encounter order and lower cost by refining the continuous trajectory variables within that sequence, showing that improvements do not require a different encounter sequence.
Across cases, the evolved programs generate and prioritize candidate encounter sequences, allocate finite computation to promising time-of-flight regions, explore multiple transfer branches, combine global search with local refinement of encounter epochs and maneuver variables, and retain DSMs only when they reduce verified cost.
Together, these results show that the evolved optimizers allocate finite computation both across encounter sequences and within each sequence’s continuous design space.

SimpleTES discovers better scientific algorithms



Scientific algorithms are the computational methods that solve scientific problems: optimization solvers, forecasters, and learned models whose quality is judged by task-specific scientific objectives. These algorithms are usually produced by hand, often after years of accumulated domain expertise and engineering. We apply SimpleTES to three such problems and find that the same evaluation-driven search procedure discovers algorithms that improve over strong baselines: a geometry-aware lasso path solver that preserves strict correctness guarantees while outperforming the expert-engineered glmnet on real datasets; a whole-brain neural-activity forecaster that outperforms a prior proprietary-model search result; and a single-cell RNA-seq denoising algorithm that generalizes across datasets. We discuss the first two in detail below. Full denoising results are reported in the Supplementary Information, where an algorithm evolved exclusively on the Pancreas dataset matches the previous state of the art on held-out PBMC (0.710.71) and establishes a new best on held-out Tabula Muris Senis Lung (0.740.74 versus 0.730.73) (Supplementary M).

SimpleTES discovers a geometry-aware lasso solver that surpasses glmnet.


The lasso regularization path is a core computational primitive in high-dimensional statistics, used in cross-validation, model selection, and large-scale regression workflows from genomics to finance. The de facto solver, glmnet [39], encodes more than a decade of expert coordinate-descent engineering: warm starts, sequential strong-rule screening [142], active-set inner loops, KKT verification, and a precision-matched switch between the covariance (p<500p<500) and naive residual (p≥500p\geq 500) updates. We ask whether evaluation-driven search, starting from a faithful C++ port of glmnet itself, can produce a strictly faster solver while preserving the same correctness guarantees. The evaluator is exact: candidate programs are self-contained C++ binaries, and a candidate is valid only if its per-λ\lambda objective gap relative to sklearn’s solution stays below 10−610^{-6} on a held-out problem, with any failure forcing the score to zero. Evolution operates exclusively on synthetic problems, scored by the geometric mean of solve times across 17 procedurally generated instances that span sample-to-feature ratio, design-matrix sparsity, active-set density, and feature correlation. Because no real dataset is ever exposed to the search, the gains reported on real data below reflect generalization rather than tuning to the test set.


Across the 11 real-world datasets in Supplementary Table 16, none seen during the search, SimpleTES discovers a solver that is 2.17×2.17\times faster than glmnet on average and 14.08×14.08\times faster than sklearn, with every reported solution passing the held-out correctness check. What makes the discovered solver notable is not just raw speed but geometry awareness: it reads the shape of each problem and adapts its algorithm accordingly. Where glmnet applies coordinate descent uniformly, SimpleTES’s solver detects the problem regime and switches solver family to match it. For moderate-dimensional, tall designs (p≤2000p\leq 2000 and n≥p/4n\geq p/4) it abandons coordinate descent for an exact LARS homotopy solver that traces the regularization path analytically, updating the active set at each kink with rank-one inverse Gram updates [34]; for wide or sparse designs (p>2000p>2000 or n<p/4n<p/4) it retains coordinate descent with strong-rule screening. This geometry-dependent switching is exactly what the speedups track: the gains peak at 9.56×9.56\times over glmnet on the tall DNA design (1700×1801700\times 180, the only case with n≫pn\gg p), where the LARS branch fires on a small active set, settle at 1.301.30–1.50×1.50\times on wide biological designs where p≫np\gg n, and reach 1.361.36–1.76×1.76\times on large mixed-shape datasets such as RCV1 and Gisette. The vs-sklearn gains are largest on the biological datasets, up to 50.77×50.77\times on TCGA BRCA. In effect, the discovered program recombines two well-known but historically separate lasso solver families into a single geometry-aware policy that selects the right one for each input, arrived at from no prior beyond the starting code and the evaluator. That the speedups hold on unseen real data suggests it exploits genuine problem structure rather than fitting the synthetic surrogate distribution.




SimpleTES discovers new state-of-the-art predictor for Zebrafish whole-brain neural-activity.


Forecasting the neural activity of an entire vertebrate brain is a central challenge for understanding how brains turn sensory input and internal state into behavior [3]. Continuous whole-brain recording at single-cell resolution is limited by motion artifact [175], photobleaching and phototoxicity [72], and the trade-off between imaging speed and field-of-view [109]. Predictive models bridge this gap by learning from recorded activity and stimulus context to forecast future brain states. The Zebrafish Activity Prediction Benchmark (ZAPBench) [88], built from a two-hour light-sheet recording of a larval zebrafish exposed to a sequence of visual stimuli, provides activity traces for 71,72171{,}721 neurons over 7,8797{,}879 time steps across nine stimulus conditions, with the task of predicting neural activities up to 3232 steps ahead from only 44 steps of context. The strongest previously reported forecaster was discovered by Empirical Research Assistance (ERA) [9], a tree-search method guided by a proprietary frontier model; ERA and SimpleTES differ in both the search algorithm and the underlying model, and we ask whether SimpleTES with an open-sourced model can discover competitive forecasters on the same task under similar computational limits.


SimpleTES achieves the strongest forecasting performance on ZAPBench, outperforming prior methods at every evaluated horizon (Figure˜4d): its horizon-averaged test MAE of 0.02590.0259 at 32 steps improves over ERA (0.02830.0283; 8.5%8.5\% relative reduction) and the strongest ZAPBench baseline, the volumetric U-Net (0.02920.0292; 11.3%11.3\% relative reduction). Its whole-brain prediction closely matches both the spatial organization and magnitude of the recorded population response (Figure˜4a); the neuron-by-time raster preserves the dominant temporal structure of the recorded activity (Figure˜4b). The prediction error varies across stimulus conditions (Figure˜4c), and grows over the forecast horizon (Figure˜4e).
The discovered program (Figure˜4f) shows that SimpleTES improves performance by automatically identifying a compact, well-matched combination of forecasting modules and their parameterization. The decisive change is to reformulate the prediction target: rather than regressing absolute future activity, the network predicts a residual added back through an identity skip connection, echoing residual learning [53] and last-value normalization from NLinear-style models [168]. Around this residual predictor it adds an explicit linear-trend baseline, combines it with the nonlinear forecasts using per-horizon closed-form least-squares weights, and feeds the nonlinear predictor a rich per-neuron descriptor including first-order differences, window slopes, per-step population statistics, and data-driven identity features from each neuron’s low-rank SVD loadings and coupling to the brain-wide mean.

SimpleTES improves AI foundations



Figure 5: Better AI foundations discovered across GPU kernel optimization and scaling-law extrapolation. (a) GPU kernel optimization task, where the optimizer translates a high-level operator into an architecture-aware implementation and minimizes execution time on a target GPU. (b) Discovered TriMul implementation with mixed precision, fused kernels, hierarchical tiling, and memory/thread mapping. (c) Kernel speedup comparisons for trimul, asymmetric matmul, and cumsum. (d) Scaling-law prediction task, where the optimizer converts small-scale training measurements into an extrapolative symbolic law and minimizes prediction error on larger target compute scales. (e) Discovered law predicts the target-scale LR & BSZ loss landscape and selects near-optimal hyperparameters. (f) SLDBench results across models and frameworks, where higher accuracy indicates better performance.


Two important foundations of modern AI development are building efficient GPU kernels that make models run fast on real hardware (Figure˜5a), and discovering scaling laws that help predict how model performance changes as training is scaled up (Figure˜5d). Both have traditionally relied on expert manual design: GPU kernels are carefully optimized by systems engineers for specific hardware architectures and software stacks, while scaling laws are manually specified and fitted by researchers to predict how performance changes with model size, data size, compute, and other scaling variables. We apply SimpleTES to both classes of problem and find that the same evaluation-driven search procedure produces kernels that surpass expert Triton submissions and AI kernel-discovery baselines on real hardware, and scaling laws that extrapolate substantially better than the strongest agent baselines on the SLDBench benchmark.


GPU kernel optimization.


We apply SimpleTES to optimize the GPU kernels that modern AI systems rely on. SimpleTES starts from a simple PyTorch reference implementation and searches for a faster GPU kernel that preserves numerical correctness within a task-specific tolerance. We evaluate this ability on three representative operators. The first is TriMul, a triangular multiplicative update used in AlphaFold3-class protein-structure models [1, 140] and the subject of an active GPUMode optimization competition [49]. The second is asymmetric matrix multiplication, an irregular-shape GEMM pattern in modern AI workloads, including small-batch inference, LoRA adapters, and query-similarity search. The third is batched cumulative sum, a primitive in LLM sampling and stream-compaction pipelines. Across all three tasks, SimpleTES discovers kernels on an NVIDIA H200, and the resulting implementations are evaluated without re-tuning on the target GPUs. We compare against both expert-engineered kernels and recent AI-driven kernel-discovery systems baselines that achieve previous SOTA efficiency [165, 20, 14, 30].


On TriMul, a kernel discovered by SimpleTES on H200 transfers directly to H100 without re-tuning, reaching a geometric-mean latency of 1.122 ms, surpassing both the AI baseline of 1.154 ms in Figure˜5c and the strongest expert-written Triton baseline of 1.140 ms on the GPUMode leaderboard (Supplementary Table˜12). The same implementation achieves the fastest runtime on NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, and AMD MI300, suggesting that the search found a portable implementation strategy rather than an H200-specific optimization (Supplementary Table˜13). Inspection of the discovered implementation shows that the gain comes from jointly optimizing high-level structure and low-level kernel tuning. SimpleTES fuses layer normalization, gating, projection, and masking into a small number of Triton kernels, selects a mixed-precision path in which activations move in FP16 while reductions remain in FP32, and tunes tile sizes within the kernels to improve hardware utilization (Figure˜5b). The asymmetric-matmul and batched-cumsum tasks further show that SimpleTES can specialize the implementation strategy to the input shape, rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all template for each operator. On asymmetric matrix multiplication, the largest gains occur on highly uneven matrix shapes, where SimpleTES achieves up to 4.01×4.01\times speedup over the PyTorch FP32 reference and reduces runtime by 65.6% relative to CUDA Agent on the case with the largest improvement (Figure˜5c). Batched cumulative sum provides a clearer example of shape-dependent implementation: the discovered kernel selects between single-tile and multi-tile execution paths according to workload size. This implementation outperforms NVIDIA’s hand-tuned CUB DeviceSegmentedScan on four of the six evaluated shapes and reaches 6.06×6.06\times speedup over the PyTorch reference. CUB remains only marginally faster on the two smallest shapes, where its fixed segmented-scan strategy is already well matched to the input. These case studies show that SimpleTES can automatically discover optimization strategies that are typically hand-engineered in optimized GPU libraries. Detailed shape definitions are provided in the Supplementary Tables˜9, 10 and 11.



Scaling-law discovery.


We evaluate SimpleTES on four tasks from the SLDBench benchmark [79, 78], covering parallel scaling [26], domain-mixture scaling [163], learning-rate/batch-size co-scaling [77], and U-shape compute scaling [157]. The task is to discover a symbolic law fθf_{\theta} together with a per-setting fitting procedure that extrapolates accurately to held-out larger-scale configurations, where each configuration specifies the scale variables and task-specific control variables used for fitting and evaluation. Success is measured by the extrapolation coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}) on each task’s extrapolation split. To isolate the effect of the search strategy, we use the same initialization, task instructions, and evaluator as the SLDAgent baseline [79]: the initial program is a naive power-law function paired with a BFGS optimizer. Across the four tasks (Figure˜5d, Supplementary Table˜14), SimpleTES achieves the best average R2R^{2} of 0.674, exceeding the strongest baseline (SLDAgent with GPT-5, 0.572) and every other configuration tested. The advantage is sharpest on the hardest extrapolative settings: SimpleTES achieves the highest R2R^{2} on the U-shape compute-scaling task (u_shape; −0.008-0.008, versus −0.232-0.232 for the next-best baseline) and on the learning-rate/batch-size co-scaling task (lr&bsz; 0.712 versus 0.611 for SLDAgent+o4-mini), where most agents obtain negative test-set R2R^{2} and fail to extrapolate. The discovered law on lr&bsz produces a hyperparameter recommendation only 0.058% above the true optimum at a 1B-parameter, 100B-token target setting, corresponding to a 10×\times extrapolation in model size and a 100×\times extrapolation in data size (Supplementary K).


These two task families share an interface—an initial solution and a queryable evaluator—and differ only in what the evaluator measures (wall-clock runtime under a correctness tolerance for kernels; held-out extrapolation R2R^{2} for scaling laws). What unites them substantively is that both produce artifacts that AI development itself depends on: faster kernels reduce the cost of training and serving every downstream model, and more accurate scaling laws improve the decisions made before training begins. The same evaluation-driven scaling principle that surpasses expert Triton kernels on a competition leaderboard also discovers symbolic loss laws that extrapolate where strong agent baselines do not.

From sequential refinement to independent search.


To understand the design choice of SimpleTES, we start with a simple, straightforward evaluation-driven scaling policy: sequential refinement. Specifically, it generates a candidate, evaluates it, uses all historical feedback to generate a better one, and repeats.
πseq\pi_{\text{seq}} corresponds to a special case in Definition 0.1 parameterized by (1,L,1,Φ)(1,L,1,\Phi).


Yet sequential refinement has a fundamental limitation. Open-ended problems require multidimensional coverage: a high-quality solution must simultaneously satisfy multiple criteria (correctness, efficiency, generality, etc.). But refinements are path-dependent: the direction of early attempts largely determines the space of subsequent improvements. This mismatch creates a “Matthew Effect” where early progress in one dimension attracts further refinement to that same dimension, starving alternatives and trapping the search around local optima.


To overcome this limitation, SimpleTES introduces a simple additional axis: global width CC. Specifically, we run CC independent trajectories in parallel, each maintaining its own history and exploring possible directions for improvement separately. By enabling independent exploration, global width increases the chance that at least one trajectory starts from sufficiently diverse early attempts, allowing later refinements to compound into qualitatively better solutions.


For readers interested in a formal justification of this effect, we provide a mathematical model and theorem in Supplementary C. Here, we empirically demonstrate the phenomenon by applying SimpleTES to two mathematical problems under different combinations of CC and LL. As shown in Figure˜7 (left), increasing LL initially improves performance but quickly saturates, consistent with the lock-in effect of a single refinement trajectory. In contrast, increasing CC provides a clear benefit by diversifying the committed histories explored under the same feedback-driven loop. This observation motivates global width as a key dimension of SimpleTES: before simply refining deeper, the policy should allocate evaluator queries to multiple independent trajectories.

Remark.


The theorem rigorously justifies the effect of independent experiments. This reflects a fundamental asymmetry between the two scaling factors: CC governs the exploration strength, while LL governs exploitation power.
This asymmetry is manifested clearly in practice. For instance, on the Second Autocorrelation Inequality, the strongest agent such as Claude-Code with Opus 4.6 plateaued at a score of 0.9438, even with hundreds of refinement steps at a cost of ∼100\sim 100 million tokens and ∼500\sim 500 USD. However, by effectively balancing CC and LL (method specified below), we match this score using the open-source gpt-oss-120b model222Estimated costs for gpt-oss-120b are calculated based on the median pricing from OpenRouter, which is $0.15 per 1M input tokens and $0.60 per 1M output tokens. at a cost of ∼60\sim 60 USD (8.3×8.3\times gap). More surprisingly, we achieve a SOTA score of 0.9627 by continuously scaling up the evaluation (∼400\sim 400 USD), a score that no closed-source model could improve upon. This empirical evidence clearly demonstrates the importance of identifying the correct factor for evaluation scaling.


Having demonstrated how compute should be allocated across multiple refinement trajectories, we turn to the scaling within each trajectory, with a given budget L=N/CL=N/C.
At first glance, more refinement steps seem preferable, as each step can leverage feedback from previous attempts. However, this intuition could break down when path dependence is strong (β\beta is large), when each refinement step further commits the trajectory to its current direction, making it harder to escape suboptimal regions.

To investigate the scaling behavior of SimpleTES, we explore the impact of key framework parameters: total evaluation budget NN, refinement depth LL, global width CC, and local sample size KK. We aim to reveal how the framework effectively translates increased computational scale into substantial performance improvements. In our ablation studies, we select three representative open-ended tasks—the First Autocorrelation Inequality, the Erdős Minimum-Overlap Problem, and the TriMul task in GPU kernel optimization—to investigate the scalability of SimpleTES.

Scalability of global width (CC) and refinement depth (LL).


First, we scale along the dimensions of global parallel exploration (CC) and sequential refinement depth (LL). For these experiments, we hold the local sample size constant at K=32K=32. The results are visualized in Figure˜2.


As demonstrated in the heatmaps, SimpleTES exhibits strong and consistent scalability along both the global width (CC) and sequential refinement depth (LL) axes. The consistent performance improvements observed as LL increases serve as compelling evidence for the efficacy of sequential refinement, demonstrating that iteratively leveraging historical feedback successfully drives targeted enhancements. However, because sequential refinement is inherently path-dependent and prone to saturation around local optima, scaling CC provides a critical and complementary advantage. The robust gains along the CC axis validate the power of parallel exploration: by distributing the evaluation budget across independent trajectories, the framework successfully diversifies the committed histories, effectively mitigating path-dependent bottlenecks and ensuring that later refinements compound upon structurally advantageous foundations.


Furthermore, the heatmaps reveal that the performance benefits derived from scaling CC versus scaling LL are strongly task-dependent. For mathematical discovery tasks like the First Autocorrelation Inequality and the Erdős Minimum-Overlap Problem, scaling the number of parallel chains CC (e.g., up to C=32C=32) provides a more pronounced advantage at larger scales. Mathematical constructions often require extensive exploration of diverse starting points to discover a promising structural “flash of insight.” Conversely, for the TriMul GPU kernel optimization task, scaling the iteration depth LL drives the most significant performance gains. Kernel optimization heavily relies on complex, step-by-step engineering refinement rather than sudden structural breakthroughs, making deep trajectories (large LL) essential to systematically tune hardware-specific parameters and iteratively squeeze out peak performance.



Scalability of local sample size (KK) and refinement depth (LL).


Next, we analyze the interaction between depth LL and local sample size KK by fixing the global parallelization at C=32C=32, as illustrated in Figure˜3. Along the depth dimension, performance consistently improves as LL increases across all configurations. This is expected, as deeper chains allow the policy to iteratively exploit feedback and refine the best discovered paradigms.


However, scaling the local sample size KK reveals a highly dynamic, depth-dependent behavior. At shallow chain depths (small LL), allocating more compute to KK does not yield a consistent monotonic increase in performance. In these early stages, generating a higher-quality node via a larger KK does not necessarily translate to an immediate breakthrough; the solution is still navigating broad structural choices, making the early refinement steps inherently noisy. Yet, this trend is robustly consolidated as the chain deepens. At large values of LL, scaling KK clearly and consistently drives superior final performance, which implies that, while a rigorously selected node might not immediately show a massive score advantage, it establishes a fundamentally higher-quality foundation that is more amenable to continuous improvement. As the chain extends, this early structural advantage compounds, allowing the long-term benefits of local quality control to fully materialize.


Supplementary Figure 4: Average score (lower the better) as a function of the total evaluation budget N=L×C×KN=L\times C\times K for the First Autocorrelation Inequality (left), the Erdős Minimum-Overlap Problem (middle), and the Triangular Multiplicative Update (TriMul) task (right), with the shaded region indicating the score range.



Scalability of the total evaluation budget (NN).


Building upon the previous analysis of the effects of CC, KK and LL, we further investigate the overall scaling behavior as a function of the total evaluation budget N=L×C×KN=L\times C\times K. As illustrated in Figure˜4, SimpleTES demonstrates a remarkably stable performance improvement as the available compute budget scales. This trend highlights a core strength of our framework: it does not merely consume inference tokens, but highly effectively translates an expanded evaluation budget into tangible, systematic performance gains. Crucially, this robust scaling behavior points to an important test-time scaling law for open-ended scientific discovery. It demonstrates that SimpleTES allows researchers to continuously and reliably push past existing performance upper bounds through the allocation of additional evaluation calls.
